cells.tense: The beginner's eye is open now and it is being used on what is here.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Name how the pull actually feels when you touch it, then give it fifteen minutes this week — just the first move, not the finished shape.
cells.core:
You can meet something new with your whole heart open and still keep your feet under you. The wondering is live and the shape underneath it is showing. That's the beginner's eye doing its work — seeing plainly, before habit gets a vote.
What's here is easy to fall for, and none of it has been tested. So keep it small and keep it warm. Return to whatever draws you, a little at a time — not the plan for it, the thing itself. Name how it feels when you touch it; that's information the plan can't give you. What you feed will tell you whether it wants feeding.

cells.verb: bringing the first look to what hasn't happened yet

cells.tense: The next chapter is being written in advance and hasn't been lived yet.
cells.act: learn how it grows by tending it
cells.ask: Take a plant already in your windowsill and keep it going two weeks without improving it or deciding what it's for.
cells.core:
You can picture how it goes before it goes, and lately the picture is doing the living for you. The imagining runs faster than the moment it's meant to be about. What began as a wide-open way of sensing has turned into rehearsal — you're bracing for a chapter the ink hasn't touched, and the bracing is the tell.
Come back to what grows at a rate you don't set. Tend a plant already in your windowsill for two weeks — no improving it, no deciding what it's for. Growth happens while nobody is forcing it. Learning the actual rate things change hands you back the pace you've been outrunning.
cells.sheetLine: You're living the draft of a chapter that hasn't happened.

cells.tense: The door it walked through is behind it, and it is still standing in the doorway.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Sit with one ordinary object for two full minutes — a cup, a chair, a leaf — and notice it before naming what it's for.
cells.core:
You can feel what hasn't happened yet, and lately you're not looking. Everything stays dim because the moment it would land in feels like somewhere already left behind. You're on the threshold, still deciding whether to walk in. Whatever this is made of, it's awake and it isn't being pointed anywhere.
Don't try to dream harder. Watch instead. Sit with one ordinary object for two full minutes and notice it before naming what it's for. It comes back through the senses, not through effort. Letting something finish before you label it is how the light returns for the next thing you meet.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room it is already writing, and the writing goes out unsigned.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Take something you read clearly this month and put the sequence on paper — first this, then that — with no mood words in it.
cells.core:
You see the shape underneath things, and you've been treating that as a mood rather than a skill. Ask you and you'll say the pattern simply appears, and you're just passing time. Meanwhile the people close to you get the read long before they get the story, and they know who is running it.
Method is where the credit comes back. Take something you read clearly this month and put the sequence on paper — first this, then that — with no mood word in it. Reading it back is how you hear your own judgment in your own voice. The plainness holds the authority you haven't been claiming.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person's vision has been cut off from lived experience — the record says only that they stand past an open door and haven't come through it, not what is behind them. A reader could say, correctly, that the looking might simply be their temperament, not a wound; I've kept the description to what can be seen now, with no history, no cause, no cost. The ask survives either way: listening for the pattern rather than the story is useful even if my read of the standing-still is wrong, because it costs nothing and teaches them something either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the joint in the last cell — hearing it that way costs nothing to say and lets the drafts meet; it would be cut first.
